output.title: Spot duplicate emails before they become extra work
output.body:
If you run a small business, duplicate emails are worth treating as a workflow decision, not a tech curiosity. The real question is simple: do the duplicates show up before you act on them, or only after you have already replied, filed, or forwarded something? That is the point where manual work starts to pile up.

A good first step is to look at three recent examples and write down where each duplicate came from. Was it the same person sending again, two tools syncing the same contact, or you copying a thread into another place? Then sort the cases into two groups: duplicates that must be caught before action, and duplicates that can be cleaned up later. Invoices and payment requests belong in the first group. A newsletter usually does not. Human approval stays in place for anything involving money or another high-risk decision.

If you want a practical test, spend one week routing suspicious duplicates to a single folder and review them by hand. Note how many are real repeats, how many are false positives, and how much time the review takes. If the list turns out messy, that is still useful. It means the next step is a clearer definition of “duplicate,” not a bigger tool. Sometimes the fix is less glamorous than the problem deserves.
